To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have detected variability on τ  Bootis A possibly induced magnetically by its planetary companion, which is in a 3.3 d orbit.
we have detected variability on τ  Bootis A possibly induced magnetically by its planetary companion and that this variability has been persistent over 440 planets orbits.
there is an apparently stable, variable region on τ  Boota that is synchronized to the planetary orbit and lies ~68 degrees ahead of the sub-planet point.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of the effects of the planet on the parent star.

the detection and analysis of the variability in the light of a rapidly rotating star and its Ca II K reversal line, which is caused by the passage of its giant planet across the visible disk of the star.
the possible interaction between a giant planetary companion and its parent star in a 51 Peg type system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the variable region is most likely induced on the surface of the parent star by the planetary companion.
the variable region is probably an active region induced by the planetary companion.
τ  Bootis A has an active region induced by its giant planetary companion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Ca II activity and the light curve of τ  Bootis A are consistent with an active region induced by the planetary companion, which varies on the time scale for a stellar rotation and tracks the planetary orbital period.

the MOST photometry and the ground-based Ca II K reversal data show the presence of a variable region on the stellar surface of τ  A, which tracked the planetary orbital motion for some 440 revolutions and lies $\phi=0.$8 in advance of the planetary companion.

the Ca II line reversal results and the photometric results are in excellent agreement and both point to a region on the surface that varies in brightness on a time scale of a planetary rotation and that tracks the planetary companion. © The European Southern Observatory (ESO) 200
The main takeaway from our work is that
τ  Bootis is a good case for a star with a giant planet that is interacting with the star.
the MOST satellite has the sensitivity and time coverage to detect variability induced by the planetary companion on the surface of its parent star.
the planet may be inducing a region of magnetic activity on the surface of its parent star.
